main.text: This is what Scripture says about locusts, if you except two passages, one in the Old Testament and the other in the New, whose sense is not obvious, because something mystical is thought to underlie them. The first is Eccles. XII, 7. [var. 5.], where among the various discomforts of old age, which are described by Solomon in allegorical words, one is this: ויסתבל החגב, And the locust shall grow heavy (or shall become pregnant). The Greeks, Jerome and the Arabic render the locust shall be made fat. And the Syriac has ܢܣܓܐ [נסגא], shall increase. This is the antecedent put for the consequent, since things that are fattened and enlarged are heavier. Now, what this means some of the ancients investigate anxiously. And, forgetting that an old man is the subject here, they invent many mysteries for themselves, but by the art by which anything is made out of anything. Salonius, on the locust shall be made fat: that is, the Gentile people shall believe, and shall be filled with spiritual goods. Olympiodorus, joining these words with those that precede and follow, the almond tree shall flower, the locust shall grow fat, and the caper shall open, observes that all these things truly happen. He means, therefore, that eternal life is so described, in which there will be an eternal spring. Yet the same author a little later, in a sense not only different but entirely opposite, understands by the locust that grows fat the underworld, which is fed by the punishments of sinners and in a certain way grows fat. Τροφὴν [trophēn], he says, ἡ κόλασις δέχεται τοὺς ἁμαρτωλοὺς, καὶ τρόπον τινὰ παχύνεται [hē kolasis dechetai tous hamartōlous, kai tropon tina pachynetai]. He adds, namely, that the locust is a symbol of punishments, because through it God punished the Egyptians. For R. Selomo [=Rashi (R. Solomon ben Isaac)] ויסתבל means it stood erect on its feet, which is plainly false. But he chose to render it so, in order that by the locust that stood erect might be signified the statue sixty cubits high which Nebuchadnezzar set up in the plain of Dura, Dan 3:1. Yet he imagines that it collapsed as often as it was set up, until all the gold there was in Jerusalem was poured out at its feet as tribute, so that what is said in Ezek 7:19 might be fulfilled: Their gold shall be removed. For Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim], the locust shall become heavy means it will be heavy, or it will be a burden; as if there were such weakness in the old man that he cannot bear even a locust, that is, cannot sustain even the smallest weights, since he is a burden to himself ^{R1}.

[III, 335] For others among the moderns, the locust shall grow heavy means: he who in his youth leapt like a locust is now through age so heavy that he cannot even walk [III, 336] ^{R2}. For others the old man, as an old man, is called a locust, being like a locust, because [col. 494] an old man's bones stick out and his body is wasted, so that he is a mere image of death.

[III, 337] Accordingly the poets imagine that Tithonus in extreme old age was changed into a cicada, an animal not only extremely dry and parched like a locust, but also very talkative, qualities that suit old age. Hence Horace says of him, book 1, Ode 28:

And Servius on book 1 of the Georgics: When he had wished for a longer life, he was turned into a cicada. And on book 4 of the Aeneid: Whom length of life turned into a cicada. This is imagined because, as Cicero says, (in an old man) only the voice remains, and his nature is more talkative ^{R3}. Hence in Iliad 3, line 151, two Trojan old men, Ucalegon and Antenor, who, already unfit for arms, detained the people with talk at the Scaean gates, are described as
— — τεττίγεσσιν ἐοικότες, οἵ τε καθ᾽ ὕλην, Δένδρεῳ ἐφεζόμενοι, ὅπα λειριόεσσαν ἱεῖσι, [tettigessin eoikotes, hoi te kath᾽ hylēn, Dendreō ephezomenoi, hopa leirioessan hieisi,]

Like cicadas, which in the forest, sitting on a tree, send forth a flowery voice. That is, as Eustathius writes following Plutarch, διὰ συνέχειαν λαλιᾶς [dia synecheian lalias], because of their continual talkativeness. See also Tzetzes, Chiliad 8, History 166.

There are some who, thinking a mention of the locust out of place here, hold that חגב chagab in this passage is something else. For some of the Hebrews, interchanging Cheth and Ajin, חגב is the same as עגב, that is, the pudendum, as though it were meant that this part grows languid and slack in old men. Kimchi and Aben Ezra [=Abraham ibn Ezra] rightly reject this ^{R4}. But for the latter חגב is הקרסול, the leg or the ankle. And for the Chaldee [III, 338] interpreter it is the ankle-bone of the foot; he renders Solomon's words thus: ויתנפחון אסחורי רגליך, And the ankle-bones of your feet shall swell. Others: the ankles of your feet. But that אסחורי or אסחוירי are the ankle-bones of the feet I have learned from the Gloss on the Talmud, tractate Iebamoth ch. 12, fol. 109a, where אסחוירא is defined as קבילא המפסקת בין שוק לרגל, the ankle-bone dividing the leg from the foot. קבילא is not a Hebrew word, as people think, but the French cheville, which means the ankle-bone of the foot. For the one who uses it, R. Selomo, was a Frenchman. Again in tractate Menachoth fol. 33a, we read that it is מקום חבור השוק והרגל הוי השוק זקוף מלמעלי והרגל שוכב בזה, the place where the leg joins the foot, namely with the leg raised above and the foot lying below. Hence אסחורא is often used by the Chaldee paraphrast for a step. And it corresponds to the Hebrew אשור, from which I would say it was derived, if the Chaldeans changed the Hebrew ש into ס, as the Arabs are accustomed to do. Now, to say what I think, I side with those for whom חגב chagab in this passage is not the locust but a part of the leg, inasmuch as the term leg also includes the thigh. And which part that is I think I have learned from the Arabs, for whom حجبة [ḥajaba] chagaba is the head of the thigh-bone. Golius [=Jacobus Golius, Lexicon Arabico-Latinum (1653)]: حجبة [ḥajaba] (Chagaba), the head of the hip, projecting on either side; the two are called حجبتان [ḥajabatān] chagabathani. Giggeius [=Antonio Giggei, Thesaurus linguae Arabicae (Milan 1632)]: الحجبتان [al-ḥajabatān] (Alchagabathan), each extremity of the thigh-bone and of the haunch above the groin. I understand the twin head of the thigh-bone, on account of which anatomists call it ἀμφικέφαλον [amphikephalon]. Since the movement of the leg begins from this head of the thigh-bone, Solomon rightly says of the old man, ויסתבל חגב, And the chagab grows heavy, to show that his gait is heavier and slower ^{R5}.

The other passage is in chapter nine of the Apocalypse, which deals with locusts that have some features taken from the description of the real locust. But you may see many peculiar features added to these, which pertain to the mystery. To the former I assign the fact that [col. 495] smoke casts these locusts down onto the earth. For smoke rises from the pit of the abyss, ὡς καπνὸς καμίνου μεγάλης [hōs kapnos kaminou megalēs], as the smoke of a great furnace, or, as others read, καιομένης [kaiomenēs], of a burning one; hence the Syriac ܐܝܟ ܬܢܢܐ ܕܐܬܘܢܐ [איך תננא דאתונא], and the Arabic edited at Paris تنور ملتهب [tannūr multahib]. There follows: And the sun and the air were darkened by the smoke of the pit; and out of the smoke came locusts upon the earth. It is in exactly this way that [III, 339] the Acridophagi hunt locusts, of whom Agatharchides says: Καπνῷ δὲ ταύτας θηρῶσιν, ἐκ τοῦ ἀέρος ἐπὶ γῆν καταφέροντες· [Kapnō de tautas thērōsin, ek tou aeros epi gēn katapherontes] They hunt them with smoke, bringing them down out of the air onto the ground. And Strabo: Ἐν ταῖς χαράδραις δὲ ἐμβάλλοντες ὕλην καπνώδη, καὶ ὑφάψαντες μικρόν· ὑπερπετάμεναι γὰρ τὸν καπνὸν σκοτοῦνται, καὶ πίπτουσι. [En tais charadrais de emballontes hylēn kapnōdē, kai hyphapsantes mikron; hyperpetamenai gar ton kapnon skotountai, kai piptousi.] They throw smoky material into the ravines and set it alight; and the locusts, flying over, are blinded by the darkness the smoke spreads, and fall. Whoever wants more should read Diodorus, book 3, where a deep ravine is described, extending over many stadia and filled with kindled material, which is abundantly available in those parts: Ἐγειρομένου δὲ καπνοῦ πολλοῦ, καὶ δριμέος, αἱ μὲν ἀκρίδες ὑπερπετόμεναι τὴν χαράδραν, καὶ διὰ τὴν τοῦ καπνοῦ δριμύτητα πνιγόμεναι, καταπίπτουσιν ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν, ὀλίγον διαπετασθεῖσαι τόπον· [Egeiromenou de kapnou pollou, kai drimeos, hai men akrides hyperpetomenai tēn charadran, kai dia tēn tou kapnou drimytēta pnigomenai, katapiptousin epi tēn gēn, oligon diapetastheisai topon] When much acrid smoke has been raised, the locusts, flying over the ravine and suffocated by the acridity of the smoke, fall to the ground after flying only a little way past that spot. The sacred writer seems to have alluded to this account of the Acridophagi ^{R6}. Likewise, the statement in verses 5 and 10 that they harm men for five months seems to be made because locusts, born in spring, die toward the end of summer and do not usually live beyond five months. And their description in verse 7 as like horses prepared for battle is taken from Ioelis II, 4. Their appearance is as the appearance of horses, and like horsemen they shall run. And in verse 8, Their teeth were as the teeth of lions: so we have in Ioelis I, 6. His teeth are the teeth of a lion, and he has the molars of a lioness. But also the statement in verse 9, They also had breastplates, as it were breastplates of iron, pertains in some way to the nature of locusts, of which Claudian says:
— — a covering grown with it hardens on its back; nature has armed its skin. — —

Erpenianus [=the Arabic version edited by Thomas Erpenius (Pentateuch 1622; New Testament 1616)], referring it to the wings, rendered it thus: واجنحتهم مثل اتراس حديد [wa-ajniḥatuhum mithl atrās ḥadīd] And their wings were like iron shields. The other, however, referred it to the breast: وكانت صدورها مزردة كزرد حديد [wa-kānat ṣudūruhā muzarrada ka-zard ḥadīd] And their breasts were mailed as with breastplates of iron. What follows, that the sound of their wings was as the sound of chariots, of many horses running to battle, is taken from Ioelis II, 5. Like the sound of chariots they shall leap upon the tops of the mountains, etc. as a strong people set in battle array. Thus what has been noted so far John drew from the natural history of locusts. But now more features follow that are peculiar to these. Let the first of them be that the smoke by which they are cast down [III, 340] onto the earth does not come out of the chasm of the Acridophagi, but from the pit of the abyss, which is the chasm of the underworld. 2. That they harm neither the grass of the earth nor the trees of the field, but only those men who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads. 3. That they have in their tails the stings of scorpions, with which they torment men with a torment like the torment of a scorpion when it strikes a man. 4. To these are added crowns on their heads like gold. 5. And the faces of men. 6. And the hair of women. All these marks are lacking in real locusts. Finally, real locusts have no king, Prov 30:27. But these have a king, and not one of their own kind, but the angel of the abyss, who in Hebrew is called אבדון Abaddon, and in Greek Ἀπολλύων [Apollyōn], not Ἀπόλλων [Apollōn], as the Syriac and the Ethiopic have it; both are taken from destroying. For אבד abad is the verb ἀπολλύειν [apollyein], and אבדון abaddon is ἀπώλεια [apōleia]. And if locusts had a king, this name would suit him, because [col. 496] destroying is the proper work of locusts. Hence Joel 1:11, in Hebrew אבד קציר שרה, The harvest of the field has perished. And in Greek, Ἀπώλωλε τρύγητος ἐξ ἀγροῦ [Apōlōle trygētos ex agrou], The vintage has perished from the field, destroyed, that is, by locusts. But here, as other locusts are meant, so also another destruction, far different from that which common locusts bring. Its author is the angel of the abyss, that is, the devil, who, himself long since lost, is bent on this alone: to roll and thrust us too down into the same pit of perdition. Since he does this through the agency of the locusts that John describes, it would be worthwhile to show what those locusts are and to mark them out by their characteristics; but for certain reasons we refrain from this inquiry, being about to pass on to other matters.

notes.text: Mercerus [=Jean Mercier (d. 1570), commentaries on Job and Proverbs] does not depart far from this interpretation; in his Commentary he renders these words: when even the locust shall be a burden to you, a very small creature, than which otherwise nothing is lighter. Among those who take חגב properly of the locust must also be counted Ludovicus de Dieu, who renders the Hebrew words וינאץ השקד ויסתבל החגב: although the almond tree blossoms, and the locust is laden with fat, i.e. although it is the most delightful season of the year, yet appetite will make it void (ותפר אביונה), and you will be able to derive no pleasure from it. Doederlein too, in his Scholia on the Poetical Books of the O. T. on this passage, p. 186, [III, 335] and in his German trans., thinks that the moroseness of old age is indicated by these words, although he renders the words themselves differently: the almond tree is despised (that tree is praised because it produces flowers and fruit early and before the others; as if to say, to old age even the joys of spring and of reviving nature are loathsome), and the locust makes itself troublesome; namely the locust, he says, which Anacreon also calls θέρεος προφήτης [thereos prophētēs], herald of summer, just as we noted above that the almond is put as a sign of the renewed year: this sign too, otherwise joyful, causes annoyance to the old man, who is dead to and hardened against the feeling of joys. Doederlein is followed by Io. Ern. Christ. Schmid in his German version of Ecclesiastes, entitled Salomo's Prediger, oder Koheleth's Lehren, Versuch einer neuen Uebersetzung und richtigern Erklärung, Giessen, 1794, p. 200, although in a note appended to that interpretation of the words יסתבל חגב he himself objects that it is very doubtful whether the Hebrew חגב is the same species of cicada as the Greek τεττιξ [tettix], to which they ascribe a λιγυρὴν οἴμην [ligyrēn oimēn]. But there is a weightier objection to Doederlein's interpretation: the chirping of the locust, a creature most hostile to the inhabitants of the Eastern lands, is nowhere for the poets of those peoples a herald of the most joyful season of the year, as it is for the Greek and Roman poets. This same point also tells against the opinion of Eusebius Traug. Ebert, who in his dissertation on this passage, entitled Imago Senis Salomonei ex Cap. XII. Ecclesiast., Leipzig 1770, renders our words: although the locust flits about, and the most beautiful season of the year begins. J. D. Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer], in the Programme written in the name of the Georgia Augusta Academy, by which the memory of Johann Matthias Gesner was commended to posterity, Göttingen, 1761 (which is inserted in the Syntagma Commentationum 2, Göttingen 1767), objects to the common interpretation, (remember your creator) until the locust becomes heavy, that it is ill suited to the nature of locusts and to the image of old age, since towards their old age locusts, which were previously bound to the earth, fly lightly through the air. He would therefore prefer, comparing the Arabic شبل [shabala], it grew, grew up, to render: before the locust grows up. For most kinds of locusts, he says, have a fivefold age: first true locusts, hopping and very small, break out of the eggs; then they shed their skin four times, and only after the fourth moult do they come forth winged, which is their fifth age. "As, then," Michaelis continues, "the locust through four ages either creeps or hops on the ground, a worm rather than a winged creature, and, having put off its skin for the fourth time, receives wings, and now nearer to heaven flies away, to seek an unknown shore beyond the sea: so we too throughout our whole life, divided into four ages, are bound to the earth; and when these are completed, and we are stripped of the body, we fly away to that homeland which the myths not only of the Greeks but also of the Orientals said lay beyond the vast sea, the islands of the blessed [see Michaelis, Epimetron added to Lowth's Ninth Lecture on the Sacred Poetry of the Hebrews, p. 195]. What, then, the psyche, that is the butterfly, was to the Greeks [an image of immortality, because, at first a worm bound to the earth and creeping on the ground, after a kind of sleep it would come forth winged and seek the heights; this image was richly illustrated by Io. Matth. Gesner in his Corollarium animarum Hippocratis, de illarum repraesentatione sub imagine papilionis; it is found in the Commentarii Societatis Regiae Scientiarum Goettingensis, vol. 1, p. 145 ff.], these winged locusts were to the East." Michaelis retained the same interpretation in the Supplemm. ad Lexx. [=J. D. Michaelis, Supplementa ad lexica Hebraica] Hebrr. vol. 3, p. 669 and vol. 5, p. 1711, but in such a way that in the former place he preferred to render יסתבל [III, 336] it is carried, i.e. it rises on high, it is lifted up; in the latter place, however, he returns to the notion of growing up. But rightly, in my judgement, Gottfr. Less, in the Vermischte Schriften vol. 1, p. 27 (in Essay 2, which bears the title Salomo verglichen mit Horaz [Ars poetica, vv. 169–174] und Cicero [Cato maior], vom weissen Genuss der Freuden des Lebens, nebst den zwey Gemählden des Greise-Alters und des Todes), objects to this interpretation that the usual meaning of the verb יסתבל does not fit this sense, and that it is not established from any other source that winged locusts were for the Hebrews, or for Orientals at all, an image of the passage of souls into the other life; moreover, the context of the whole discourse, which presents the troubles of advancing age in various images, stands against this interpretation. Less himself proposes two ways of interpreting: the reference is either to the hoarse voice of the cicada or to the various ages of that same creature. If the former, the words before the locust grows heavy are to be understood thus: before the voice becomes thin and fails. He prefers, however, the latter, so that חגב, the locust of the fourth age, is an image of the old man passing the last age of life, and יסתבל indicates either the failing of strength or the old man's back bent as if by a burden. But this whole interpretation rests on a very weak foundation, I might almost say on none at all, namely that חגב is the locust after its fourth moult. Much more uncertain still is the conjecture, also proposed by Less, that instead of החגב one should perhaps read ויסתבל החגם, before feasts are a burden, i.e. before one wearies of the pleasures and joys of this life. G. Zirkel, in the Untersuchungen über den Prediger, p. 361, renders our words the locust is carried, or when it is carried off, which he says happens when, having become fat and heavy, it is deprived of the power of flight and is caught and carried off by men; by this image he thinks advancing old age is described, when, as the strength of the body fails, the limbs move more slowly. A new interpretation was recently proposed by Henr. Frid. Pfannkuche in his Exercitationes in Ecclesiastae, Salomoni vulgo tributi, locum vexatissimum Cap. XI, 7.—XII, 7., Göttingen 1794. In this booklet he tried to show that that portion of Ecclesiastes contains not, as is commonly thought, a description of old age, but of every kind of misfortune and calamity, under the image of a storm with rains, gales and thunder, which is presented and variously embellished from verse 2 of Chapter XII onward. To this description of the storm also belongs, he says, the statement that small locusts (for he understands these by חגב, following Oedmann [=Samuel Ödmann, Vermischte Sammlungen aus der Naturkunde]; see above, note 5 to Chapter I) are swept away by whirlwinds, or carried off; with the vowel points changed, of course, he reads יִסָּתֵבַל החגב, the locust is carried off, is swept away (by the winds, which are hostile to locusts). Whether this arbitrary change of reading, devised in favour of a hypothesis that is hardly firm, will win everyone's approval, we very much doubt.
notes.label: R1

notes.text: In a similar way Schmidius in his Notes on this passage: the limbs, which formerly, in lively youth, were nimble like the locust, a leaping animal, now, as if weighed down by some burden, can no longer move. And Herm. Witsius in the Exercitat. in Cap. XII. Eccles. (in his Miscellanea Sacra, vol. 2, Exercitation 6), §. 22, for whom the locust denotes the limbs which in their natural state are lighter and more agile than the rest and raise themselves of their own accord (e.g. the head), but in old age grow limp, sink down and need support. Io. Bern. Koehler also takes these words of the old man's back, bent [III, 337] like a locust, in the Observatt. critice. ad Ecclesiastae Caput ultimum, in the Repertorium Literaturae biblicae et Orientalis edited by Eichhorn, vol. 16, p. 222, following Glassius (Phil. S. book 5, p. 488) and Geierus.
notes.label: R2

notes.text: "Those who have thought of Tithonus, the old man changed into a cicada, have by a manifest error confused the cicada, a very different animal, with the locust; to say nothing of the fact that Tithonus is imagined as shrunken by old age and leanness, whereas for Solomon the locust either grows, or grows fat and is weighed down." So J. D. Michaelis in the Laudatio funebris Gesneri, p. 182 of the book cited above.
notes.label: R3

notes.text: Paulus [=H. E. G. Paulus, Clavis über die Psalmen (1791) and Clavis über den Jesaias (1793)], the theologian of Jena, holds that חגב is the stomach (in his commentary on Ecclesiastes entitled Neuer Versuch über die Koheleth, in the Repertorium Literat. bibl. et orient. edited by himself, vol. 1), no doubt comparing (for he gave no reason for the German version given loc. cit.) the Arabic حُجَّابٌ [ḥujjābun], plural حُجُبٌ [ḥujubun], which among other things means the dia- [III, 338] phragm, as Golius reports, p. 577. For he translates the whole clause thus, p. 250: So lange man nicht schwer am Magen trägt, und seine Lust zum Essen schwinden sieht; so that the words יסתבל החגב would literally mean: the diaphragm will be heavy.
notes.label: R4

notes.text: Not very different from this view is what Jerome has in his Commentary on this passage: It should be known that where our manuscripts read locust, the Hebrew has chagab, a word which is ambiguous among them. For it can be rendered both ankle and locust. It indicates the swollen legs of old men, weighed down by the swellings of gout.
notes.label: R5

notes.text: For Eichhorn, in his Commentary on this passage, the smoke rising from the pit is the swarm of locusts itself, which from a distance presents the appearance of a dense cloud, or of smoke.
notes.label: R6
